title: Open problem: convex drawings vs. pseudocircular drawings
statement_text: The relation between convex drawings and pseudocircular drawings remains open.
context_text: All drawings are simple topological drawings of the complete graph $K_n$ in the plane or on the sphere: vertices are distinct points, edges are simple curves joining their endpoints and containing no other vertex, every two edges share at most one point (a common endpoint or a proper crossing), and no three edges cross at a point. The three edges among three vertices (a triangle) do not cross, so they split the plane into two sides (closures of the two components); a side is convex if every edge with both endpoints in it is drawn entirely inside it. A drawing is convex if every triangle has a convex side, and hereditary-convex if one can choose a convex side for each triangle so that whenever a triangle lies inside the chosen convex side of another triangle, its own chosen side does too (convex drawings form the second level of the convexity hierarchy of Arroyo, McQuillan, Richter and Salazar, between topological and hereditary-convex drawings). A drawing is pseudocircular if its edges can be extended to pseudocircles (simple closed curves) such that any two pseudocircles either cross exactly twice or are disjoint; it is pseudospherical if moreover every two pseudocircles intersect and, for any two edges $e\neq f$, the pseudocircle extending $e$ crosses $f$ at most once. Arroyo, Richter and Sunohara gave a topological drawing that is not pseudocircular and proved that the hereditary-convex drawings are exactly the pseudospherical drawings. The analogous relation for (non-hereditary) convex drawings, e.g. whether they are characterized by some class of pseudocircular drawings, has not been established.
